title: Hear the TV Clearly Without Blasting the Volume
subtitle: Wireless TV headphones, dialogue speakers and a few free settings can bring the words back without shaking the walls.
excerpt: If the music is loud but the words are mumbled, turning up the TV rarely helps. Here are the headphones, dialogue speakers and free TV settings that make speech easier to follow.
author: Nickel And Gadget Editors

sections.content: It is one of the most common living-room complaints: the music swells, the explosions rattle the windows, and the one line of dialogue that explains the plot slips right by. So the volume goes up, and up again, until everyone else in the house is leaving the room.

Turning up the TV makes everything louder, not just the voices. The better fix is to bring speech closer to you or make it stand out from the background. There are a few good ways to do that, and some of them cost nothing.
Your options, from free to plugged-in

A small transmitter plugs into the TV's audio output and sends the sound to a headset. You set your own volume while the TV speakers stay at a comfortable level for everyone else. Sennheiser's RS models, for example, use the transmitter as a charging dock, so the headset goes back on the stand when the show ends.

A compact speaker such as Zvox's AccuVoice line sits in front of the TV and focuses on making voices clearer rather than simply louder. Zvox describes its AccuVoice processing as using hearing aid technology, with several levels of voice boost you can step through on the remote. This works well when the whole household watches together and nobody wants to wear headphones.

If you already wear hearing aids, ask about a TV streamer made for your brand. Phonak, for instance, says its TV Connector streams TV and music directly to its hearing aids, turning Bluetooth-enabled aids into a wireless stereo headset. Compatibility depends on the exact model, so your hearing care professional is the right person to ask.

items: A connection that matches your TV. Most of these plug into an optical (digital) audio jack or a 3.5mm headphone jack; check the back of the set before you buy.
Separate volume for each ear, if one ear hears better than the other.
Several levels of voice boost on a speaker, so you can start low and turn it up only as needed.
Simple controls: large, labeled remote buttons or a single volume dial.
A charging dock for headphones, so they are always ready.
A home trial or easy return window, since what sounds clear varies a lot from person to person.

sections.content: Before buying anything, look in your TV's sound menu for a dialogue or speech setting. On a Roku TV, Roku's support pages say you can press the Star button on the remote while a show is playing, choose Sound settings, and turn on Dialog enhancement or, on some TVs, Speech clarity. Speech clarity offers Auto, Off, Low and High. Other TV and soundbar brands have similar settings under names like dialogue mode or voice enhancement.

Captions help too, even if you only glance at them. On a Roku device, go to Home, then Settings, then Accessibility (or Captions), and set Captions mode. Roku's options include On always, On replay, and on some devices On mute. Under Caption style you can make the text larger, change its color and add a solid background so it is easier to read. Some apps, such as Netflix and Hulu, have their own caption controls inside the app.

When you set up headphones or a dialogue speaker, start with the TV's own speakers turned down or off, then raise the new device until voices are clear. With a dialogue speaker, try the lowest voice-boost level first and step up only if you need to.

sections.label: Good to Know
sections.content: The National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders lists difficulty listening to TV or radio among its screening questions for hearing loss, and says about one in three people ages 65 to 74 has hearing loss. If the TV is a struggle most nights, it is worth having your hearing checked by your doctor or an audiologist.

Clearer TV sound is often a mix of small changes: a dialogue setting switched on, captions sized so you can read them, and maybe a speaker or headset that puts the words where you can hear them. Start with what is free, then add a gadget if you still find yourself reaching for the volume.

products.name: RS 120-W Wireless TV Headphones
products.price: About $129.99 (Sennheiser US store price, October 2026; listed down from $159.95)
products.blurb: A straightforward pick for one listener. Sennheiser lists up to about 200 feet of range and up to 20 hours per charge, and the transmitter doubles as the charging stand.

products.name: RS 5200 Wireless TV Headphones
products.price: About $229.95 (Sennheiser US store price, October 2026; listed down from $299.95)
products.blurb: Stethoscope-style earphones with a built-in Speech Clarity feature and separate volume for each ear, which suits listeners who hear differently on each side.

products.name: AccuVoice AV100 TV Speaker
products.blurb: A small 10-inch speaker with six levels of voice boost plus SuperVoice, connected by one cable. Zvox offers a 60-day home trial.

products.name: AccuVoice AV157 TV Speaker
products.blurb: Zvox recommends this model for more significant hearing difficulty. It has 12 voice-boost levels, output leveling to tame loud commercials, and a remote with large, labeled buttons.
